title: Effects of architectural interventions on psychological, cognitive, social, and pro-environmental aspects of occupant well-being: Results from an immersive online study
research_question: To evaluate the influence of built features (natural vs. artificial materials, presence vs. absence of windows, and diverse vs. non-diverse photographic decor) on four well-being outcomes: sense of belonging, stress, creativity, and pro-environmental concern, using an immersive online study.

participants.description: Participants were located in the United States and over 18 years of age. Demographics included 60.6% men, 38.4% women, 0.5% non-binary, 0.5% prefer not to say. Mean age 37.5 years (SD 12.3). Race: 70.8% White, 8.5% Asian, 7.8% Black/African American, 5.1% Latinx, 6.8% Multiple. Education: 55.5% Bachelor's or higher, 44.0% less than Bachelor's.
participants.recruitment: Recruited from Prolific, an online crowdsourcing platform.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: 40-second panoramic video of one of eight indoor workplace conditions (2x2x2 factorial design: Natural vs. Artificial materials, Presence vs. Absence of windows, Diverse vs. Non-Diverse photographic decor).
Multiple pictures of the indoor space, including a full view as survey background and close-ups of framed photographs (diversity cues) during refresher tasks.
A paragraph describing the assigned indoor space (e.g., materials, windows, decor) was presented at the start of the survey.

measures.instrument: Revised Sense of Social and Academic Fit scale (6 items)
3-item stress scale (10-point Likert), Valence (7-point Likert), Arousal (7-point Likert)
Positive and Negative Affect Schedules (PANAS) scale (10 adjectives)
Positive and Negative Affect Schedules (PANAS) scale (10 adjectives)
Donation to tree-planting organization from $50 raffle winnings

mechanisms: Diverse representation signaled an inclusive environment, leading to psychological safety and conditions conducive to creative thinking.
The rephrasing of belonging questions to explicitly refer to the study environment (vs. research institution) might explain new findings.
Experiencing physical contact with natural materials might affect different components of stress than seeing pictures of them.
The online stressor might have been too small to yield significant differences in pre-post stress measures.
Pathways through which diverse representation reduces stress might require physical exposure.
Additional exposure to diversity pictures during refresher tasks might have stimulated increased creativity.
Short exposure duration in the online survey might not be sufficient for built features to affect pro-environmental concern outcomes.
implementation_implications: The presence of windows, natural materials, and diverse representation in built environments can positively impact occupant well-being (belonging, stress, creativity).

Immersive online surveys are an effective and efficient experimental paradigm for built environment research, offering advantages in cost, time, human resources, flexibility, and participant diversity.
Future research should investigate the quantity of built elements (e.g., number of wooden elements, window size) beyond mere presence/absence.

limitations: Inability to control participants' actual built environment during the online survey (e.g., presence of natural light, ambient sounds, other people).
Online studies are not well-suited for testing tactile and olfactory aspects of the built environment.
Photographs/videos cannot fully reproduce biological benefits of true natural light or negative effects like thermal discomfort/glare from windows.
Limited exposure duration (<1 hour) in the short online study might not be sufficient to elicit variations in some well-being outcomes.
The study design only investigated presence/absence of features, not their quantity (e.g., number of wooden elements, size of windows).

paper_metadata.title: Disembodied Worlds – Body, Brain and Architecture in the Digital Age: A Conversation with Psychobiologist Vittorio Gallese
paper_metadata.crossref_title: Disembodied Worlds – Body, Brain and Architecture in the Digital Age: A Conversation with Psychobiologist Vittorio Gallese
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: AbstractGuest‐Editor Ian Ritchie has a conversation with Vittorio Gallese, Professor of Psychobiology at the University of Parma, Italy, whose research focuses on neurophysiology, cognitive neuroscience, social neuroscience and philosophy of mind. Gallese is one of the discoverers of mirror neurons. Here he describes how they relate to empathy and our understanding of ourselves and others.
